Series::extract_put¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::extract_put(pluss::RangeView<ExtractSpec> specs, const Series& values) const -> Series

What It Does¶

Returns a patched copy after writing through the full selector language.

This is the value-semantic sibling of extract_put_(). The selector grammar is the same, the write cardinality rules are the same, and the logical write order is the same. The difference is ownership:

  • extract_put_() mutates the current Series

  • extract_put() leaves the current Series unchanged and returns a new one

That makes extract_put() the right surface when the write belongs inside an expression, a pipeline, or any place where “derive a modified result” is clearer than “mutate this object first.”

Parameters¶

specs (pluss::RangeView<ExtractSpec>)

The destination selector.

This method accepts the same selector family as extract():

  • scalar indices

  • slices, including negative-step slices

  • SliceAll()

  • Ellipsis()

  • NewAxis()

  • bool masks

  • integer index Series

Write-side interpretation is the load-bearing point:

  • scalar indices narrow the addressed region

  • slices preserve an axis and choose positions on it

  • Ellipsis() expands to the needed identity slices

  • NewAxis() is accepted for selector compatibility, but does not create a new writable destination dimension

  • advanced selectors are materialized into explicit destination positions

values (const Series&)

The source values to write into the selected destinations.

Two value modes are supported:

  • scalar source: broadcast across the entire selection

  • non-scalar source: values.numel() must exactly match the number of selected destination elements

As on the in-place sibling, matching is by selected element count rather than by preserving the visible shape of values.

Returns¶

Series A new Series containing the write result.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shared setup. Start from a grid whose state is easy to track.

auto copy_grid = pluss::make_series({
    {100.0, -1.0, 12.0, 13.0},
    {200.0, 70.0, 22.0, 90.0},
    {300.0, -1.0, 32.0, 33.0},
});

std::cout << copy_grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[100, -1, 12, 13],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [300, -1, 32, 33]]

Example 2. A scalar source broadcasts across the selected region of the returned copy.

auto patched = copy_grid.extract_put(
    {pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(2, 4, 1)},
    pluss::make_series(5.0));

std::cout << patched;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[100, -1, 5, 5],
  [200, 70, 5, 5],
  [300, -1, 5, 5]]

Example 3. The original input is unchanged after the copy-returning write.

std::cout << copy_grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[100, -1, 12, 13],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [300, -1, 32, 33]]

Example 4. Bool masks can patch only the rows that satisfy the mask.

auto row_mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true});

std::cout << copy_grid.extract_put(
                 {row_mask, pluss::Slicing::SliceAll()},
                 pluss::make_series(0.0));

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0, 0, 0],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [0, 0, 0, 0]]

Example 5. Reverse slices are also legal on the copy-returning surface.

std::cout << copy_grid.extract_put(
                 {std::int64_t{1}, pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(-1, pluss::Slicing::Slice::kUnbounded, -2)},
                 pluss::make_series({900.0, 700.0}));

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[100, -1, 12, 13],
  [200, 700, 22, 900],
  [300, -1, 32, 33]]

The selector visits row 1, columns 3 then 1, and the source values are consumed in that same order.

Example 6. Integer index Series selectors can patch explicit rows by copy.

auto picked_rows = pluss::make_series({2LL, 0LL});

std::cout << copy_grid.extract_put(
    {picked_rows, pluss::Slicing::SliceAll()},
    pluss::make_series({
        {9000.0, 9001.0, 9002.0, 9003.0},
        {7000.0, 7001.0, 7002.0, 7003.0},
    }));

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[7000, 7001, 7002, 7003],
  [200, 70, 22, 90],
  [9000, 9001, 9002, 9003]]

Example 7. Invalid slice steps fail before the copy can be produced.

try {
  std::cout << copy_grid.extract_put(
                   {pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(0, 4, 0)},
                   pluss::make_series(0.0));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::extract: step cannot be 0

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • extract_put() is copy-returning. The original object stays unchanged.

  • NewAxis() is accepted as part of selector normalization, but it does not create a new writable destination axis.

  • Reverse slices, masks, and integer index selectors are all legal because this method is willing to materialize destination positions.

  • Cardinality is checked against the number of selected destination elements, not against the visible destination layout.

Summary¶

Use extract_put() when you want the richest selector-language write surface but also want value semantics. If the selector needs masks, reverse traversal, or integer advanced selectors, this is the broadest copy-returning method in the family.
